record.title: The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm at High Depth for MaxCut on Large-Girth Regular Graphs and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick Model
record.locator: Section 6 of the full preprint supplies the proof of the fixed-depth transfer; eventual Parisi optimality remains a conjecture in this antecedent.

aligned_passages.text:
The full-support manuscript proves that an admissible integrable minimizer
of the zero-temperature Parisi functional for the pure zero-field
Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model has Stieltjes support equal to every overlap
scale in [0,1). The proof turns a hypothetical support gap into a constant
interval for the order parameter. Variational contact at the ends of that
interval conflicts with a strict curvature inequality inside it. Along the
auxiliary diffusion, the spatial gradient of the value function is a bounded
martingale. Full support makes this martingale's second moment equal to time;
its terminal correlation with Brownian motion gives the ground-state value.
The manuscript's further argument gives a smooth Stieltjes density, strictly
positive on $(0,1)$, and no atom at zero. Sections 9.1–9.2 derive this stronger
ordinary conclusion separately from the selected formal support statement.

This record reconstructs those arguments and follows the finite Gaussian
approximation into the separate QAOA manuscript. The latter claims that
finite deterministic circuits approach the SK optimum when system size tends
to infinity before circuit depth increases. Its circuit construction needs
additional approximation, synthesis, seed-removal and transfer arguments.
The two formal statements concern full support and scalar value
consequences; neither states QAOA circuit convergence. Their verification
scope is described at the end. See [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main] and
[OpenAI (2026b), Theorem 1.1][q-intro].

On a single spin, let $Z=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$ and
$X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$; $Z_i$ and $X_i$ act on spin $i$
and as the identity on the other spins. Also set
$Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$ and
$|\pm\rangle=(|0\rangle\pm|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$.
Then $X|\pm\rangle=\pm|\pm\rangle$ and $Z|+\rangle=|-\rangle$. The cost and mixer are
$$
C_{n,J}=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}Z_iZ_j,\qquad B_n=\sum_iX_i.
$$
The two evolutions act differently:
$$
e^{-i\theta C_{n,J}}|\sigma\rangle
 =e^{-i\theta H_n(\sigma)}|\sigma\rangle,
\qquad
e^{-i\beta B_n}=\prod_{i=1}^n(\cos\beta\,I-i\sin\beta\,X_i).
$$
The cost evolution changes phases while preserving spin-basis probabilities;
the mixer combines amplitudes of different spin configurations. Cost evolution
alone leaves the initial uniform probabilities unchanged, and a mixer applied
first only multiplies $|+\rangle^{\otimes n}$ by $e^{-in\beta}$.
Alternating them lets the cost-dependent phases change subsequent measurement
probabilities. [Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann and Zhou (2022), §2,
equations (1)–(6)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.08187v4).

A depth-$p$ state, with $p$ counting cost–mixer pairs, is
$$
|\psi_{n,p,J}(\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta)\rangle
=e^{-i\beta_pB_n}e^{-i\gamma_pC_{n,J}}\cdots
 e^{-i\beta_1B_n}e^{-i\gamma_1C_{n,J}}|+\rangle^{\otimes n}.
$$
Here the real angle vectors $\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta$ are
deterministic; $\boldsymbol\gamma$ is separate from the Parisi coefficient
$\gamma(t)$. A *word* means a finite ordered product of cost and mixer
exponentials. Its pattern and angles are fixed independently of $n,J$;
its cost operator depends on $n,J$. Define
$$
v_p(\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta)
=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\mathbb E_J
 \langle\psi_{n,p,J}|C_{n,J}|\psi_{n,p,J}\rangle,
\qquad Q_p=\sup_{\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^p}v_p.
$$
The fixed-depth, fixed-angle infinite-size limit is the input from
Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann and Zhou; it does not contain the later depth
conclusion; see [Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann and Zhou (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.08187v4).
The source target is $\lim_{p\to\infty}Q_p=P_*$. Its needed lower
bound has the literal quantifiers
$$
\forall\varepsilon>0\quad\exists p\in\mathbb N,
\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^p:
\quad\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\mathbb E_J
\langle\psi_{n,p,J}|C_{n,J}|\psi_{n,p,J}\rangle
\ge P_*-\varepsilon.
$$
The same finite list of gates and angles is used for every $n,J$; this is
a limiting expected-energy conclusion. A cost expectation is bounded above by its
maximum eigenvalue, and zero-angle padding makes $Q_p$ nondecreasing.
It therefore suffices to construct one finite word for every accuracy.
Fixed-instance convergence at increasing depth is a different quantifier
order. Farhi, Goldstone and Gutmann's original QAOA argument obtains that
convergence by adiabatic evolution and its Trotter approximation, with depth
allowed to depend on the instance; it does not supply the size-independent
word required here. [Farhi–Goldstone–Gutmann (2014), equation (10) and
§VI, pp. 10–11](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.4028v1);
[OpenAI (2026b), Theorem 1.1][q-intro].

The construction first describes local operations on a large tree, where
neighbouring subtrees supply Gaussian inputs. Temporary random labels let
those operations implement the finite classical function of §7. The hard
steps are to implement its aggregations using cost and mixer gates, and
then to replace every use of the labels by ordinary gates while preserving
the energy. Only the resulting ordinary word is transferred to SK.

The choices are nested: fix $\varepsilon$, choose $T<1$, choose a finite
mesh, fix the bounded classical formula and helper probabilities, then
choose the finite gate approximations and remove the seeds. The constants
in a replacement may depend on the surrounding word and on those positive
helper probabilities. [§8.6](#qaoa-assembly-detail) collects the error
allocation before the final $n\to\infty$ limit.
The principal circuit inputs can be read as four local lemmas. Their
proofs remain in the cited manuscript; §§8.2–8.5 reconstruct the
mechanisms and show where each hypothesis enters.

**Smooth replacement.** Fix the height, a finite expression and channel
list, and the required derivatives. Uniform recursive weighted bounds,
convergence of operators and adjoints, and strongly commuting signals with
the stated joint exponential bounds permit substitution inside a fixed
surrounding sequence in the exclusion-gate class defined in §8.2. Constants depend on that fixed family. This is the input
used in §8.3 to replace classical aggregates by finite gates; see
[the foundations, smooth topology and gate calculus][q-gate-calculus].

**Helper contraction and synthesis.** Fix a bounded, finite, type-excluded
odd formula, zero on helpers, and positive helper masses. The contraction
converges smoothly at every cut and for the specified responses. For each
$\eta>0$, finite seeded synthesis gives
$$
\mathcal E(v)\ge\mathcal E(m)-2\eta-2\sqrt{p_H}.
$$
Section 8.4 receives this one fixed seeded word. The source inputs are the
[synthesis statements][q-synthesis-statement] and
[helper theorem][q-helper-statement].

**Seed removal.** Fix that finite seeded word and an energy tolerance.
Reuse the same Gaussian at every occurrence on a vertex. Packet control and
the one-particle comparison then produce one finite ordinary word with the
required energy error. The [seed-removal theorem][q-seed-statement] supplies
an energy conclusion, not merely convergence of seed marginals. It makes the
ordinary-word transfer in §8.5 applicable.

**Fixed-word transfer.** Fix one ordinary word and all its angles before
either size or degree varies. Its positive tree scaled-edge limit equals
its SK expected-energy limit, with the convention conversion in §8.5.
This [fixed-word transfer][q-transfer] closes the thermodynamic-first
theorem in §8.6.

**One cost–mixer pair.** A single cost–mixer pair fixes the energy normalization before we introduce the rooted representation. Use the positive cost $C_{n,J}$ of §8 and $U=e^{-i\beta B_n}e^{-i\theta C_{n,J}}$; the symbol $\theta$ here is a cost angle, not the Parisi coefficient. Put $c=\cos(2\beta)$ and $s=\sin(2\beta)$. The Pauli identities are $$ e^{i\beta X}Ze^{-i\beta X}=cZ+sY,\qquad e^{i\alpha Z_iZ_j}Y_je^{-i\alpha Z_iZ_j} =Y_j\cos(2\alpha)+Z_iX_j\sin(2\alpha). $$ The mixed term $Z_iY_j$ therefore has cost-state expectation $$ \sin(2\theta J_{ij}/\sqrt n) \prod_{k\ne i,j}\cos(2\theta J_{jk}/\sqrt n). $$ The other mixed term exchanges $i$ and $j$. The $Z_iZ_j$ term has zero expectation. The $Y_iY_j$ term can be nonzero on an individual complete graph, but its expectation after the cost gate is independent of $J_{ij}$: $Y_iY_j$ commutes with that edge cost. Multiplying by $J_{ij}$ and averaging therefore removes it, even in the presence of triangles. For a standard Gaussian $J$, $$ \mathbb E\cos(aJ)=e^{-a^2/2},\qquad \mathbb E[J\sin(aJ)]=ae^{-a^2/2}. $$ Averaging the mixed terms and summing the $n(n-1)/2$ unordered edges gives $$ \frac1n\mathbb E_J\langle C_{n,J}\rangle =\frac{n-1}{n}\,\theta\sin(4\beta) e^{-2\theta^2(n-1)/n}. $$ This agrees with [Farhi et al., equation (62)][fggz]. With energy maximization, $\theta=1/2$, $\beta=\pi/8$ gives the limiting value $1/(2\sqrt e)$; their minimization example uses $\beta=-\pi/8$ and the negative value. For the positive cost $D^{-1/2}\sum_{\{i,j\}}Z_iZ_j$ on the $(D+1)$-regular tree, each endpoint has $D$ other neighbours. The same calculation now has no common-neighbour contribution and yields $$ \langle Z_oZ_v\rangle =\sin(4\beta)\sin(2\theta/\sqrt D) \cos^D(2\theta/\sqrt D). $$ Multiplying by $\sqrt D/2$ and letting $D\to\infty$ gives $\theta e^{-2\theta^2}\sin(4\beta)$, the same limit as finite SK. This checks the factor $1/2$ and the degree convention in §8.5. The value just obtained will be recovered once more from the [rooted insertion in §8.1.1](#depth-one-rooted). That calculation explains which part of the limiting state carries the energy.

### 8.5 Transfer of the resulting ordinary word After all these choices there is one finite ordinary word $W$, fixed independently of degree, size and disorder. On the $(D+1)$-regular tree use $C_D=D^{-1/2}\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}Z_iZ_j$, counting each edge once. The edge expectation is defined on the finite light cone described in §8.1. The source applies the fixed-word transfer theorem $$ v_W=\lim_{D\to\infty}\frac{\sqrt D}{2} \langle+|W_D^*Z_iZ_jW_D|+\rangle. $$ The [full preprint of Basso et al., arXiv:2110.14206v3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14206v3), Theorem 1, equates the limiting tree recursion with the infinite-size SK recursion for every fixed depth and fixed angle vector. Its proof is in §6, especially (6.6)–(6.31), with the symmetry statement proved in Appendix B and the iteration stabilisation in Appendix A.4. The shorter proceedings edition states the theorem but refers to this full preprint for the proof. Basso et al. use a negative tree cost in (2.3). Let $V=\prod_{i\in A}X_i$ on one bipartition of the finite light cone. Every edge has exactly one endpoint in $A$, hence $$ VZ_iZ_jV=-Z_iZ_j,\qquad VB_DV=B_D,\qquad V|+\rangle=|+\rangle. $$ Consequently, if $C_D^-=-C_D$, then $VW(C_D^-,B_D)V=W(C_D,B_D)$ for the same fixed word and angles, while its measured edge expectation changes sign. This converts the negative cut convention in their (2.6) to the positive energy above. Their SK cost (6.1) already has the positive convention used here. The result applies after seed removal; it does not directly transfer an arbitrary seeded or controlled word. It also supplies no joint limit in which depth or angles change with $D$ or $n$. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, “Fixed-word transfer”][q-transfer]. For an ordinary cost or mixer the root updates are, respectively, $$ u\longmapsto e^{-itZq(v_Z)}u, \qquad u\longmapsto e^{-i\beta X}u, \qquad v_Z=u^*Zu\,\mathrm{vac}. $$ The source proves smooth convergence for these updates, their adjoints and fixed angle derivatives. The resulting occupation bounds supply the hypothesis of the root-shift energy proposition in §8.1. Thus its energy is the scaled edge limit required for transfer. Finally merge consecutive gates of the same type and insert zero-angle gates where needed to express $W$ in alternating QAOA form. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, “Ordinary root updates”][q-ordinary-updates].

### 8.6 Fixing the word before the thermodynamic limit **Approximating a specified finite observable.** First fix $T,N$ and the positive finite normalizers in §7. The rooted construction in §8.1 has energy exactly $S_{T,N}$. Let $z$ be a smoothed version of its rounded spin $F_N$, let $m=\sin(2\theta)$ be the bounded formula's spin output, and let $m^{\mathrm{col}}$ be its color-excluded approximation. Write $$ \delta_s=\|z-F_N\|_2,\qquad \delta_b=\|m-z\|_2,\qquad \delta_c=\|m^{\mathrm{col}}-m\|_2. $$ These measure errors of the spin outputs, not of the angles. The rooted shift is a contraction, so $$ |\mathcal E(f)-\mathcal E(g)| \le(\|f\|_2+\|g\|_2)\|f-g\|_2. $$ All these outputs have norm at most one. Apply synthesis with tolerance $\eta_s$ and total helper probability $p_H$, then remove the seeds with energy tolerance $\eta_r$. The source's absolute synthesis bound and seed-removal theorem, followed by fixed-word transfer, give one ordinary word $W$ with $$ |v(W)-S_{T,N}| \le2(\delta_s+\delta_b+\delta_c) +2\eta_s+2\sqrt{p_H}+\eta_r. \tag{8.2} $$ The bounded formula is chosen before the colors and helper law. The excluded receiver and ancestor colors prevent a dependency from returning through a traversed branch; reserved helper colors are absent from every dependency and the output is zero on helpers. Color refinement and small positive helper probabilities jointly control $\delta_c$ and $p_H$. Only then is synthesis performed with that law fixed, using the same sitewise Gaussian seed at every seed gate. Each term in (8.2) can thus be made smaller than its allotted tolerance in this order. [OpenAI (2026b), Lemmas 3.1–3.4][q-classical]; [synthesis energy bound][q-synthesis-statement]; [seed removal][q-seed-statement]. This establishes an absolute approximation of each specified finite $S_{T,N}$ in the construction, without assuming it is already near $P_*$. It preserves the energy; it does not assert reproduction of the entire classical output law. Near-optimality now adds the cutoff and mesh choices. Allocate errors after choosing the desired $\varepsilon>0$. Apply the classical near-optimality proposition with the two tolerances $\varepsilon/4$ and $\eta_H=(\varepsilon/8)^2$. It supplies one formula and its helper law together, with classical loss below $\varepsilon/4$ and $0P_*-3\varepsilon/4. $$ Seed removal uses less than $\varepsilon/4$. The resulting fixed ordinary word therefore satisfies $v_W>P_*-\varepsilon$ after the fixed-word transfer. Its thermodynamic limit is taken only after all approximation choices have been made. Since $Q_p\le P_*$ and zero padding makes $Q_p$ nondecreasing, this proves the source's thermodynamic-first conclusion from its stated analytic inputs. [OpenAI (2026b), §6][q-assembly]. The order is: accuracy; minimizer and fixed $T<1$; finite scalar mesh; smoothing and bounded approximations; finite types and positive helper masses; exact helper contractions and finite commutator products; one fixed seeded word; initialization size; generic angle perturbation; finite selective pulse lists; sufficiently small $r$; one ordinary word; its $n\to\infty$ limit. The degree limits identify the rooted calculus and the transferred value for each already fixed word; they do not license changing that word with the finite instance. The reconstruction makes the source's circuit mechanisms explicit, but the evidence classes remain separate. The scalar construction and its formal interfaces in §§6–7 and 12 do not by themselves establish the weighted unitary calculus, simultaneous helper contraction or seed removal. Those analytic theorems are additional inputs from the QAOA manuscript, with the domain, commutation and uniformity hypotheses specified above. No quantitative depth bound, finite-size rate, efficient angle-selection procedure, or independent formal verification of this entire circuit construction follows from the selected formal statements. This completes the main support-to-circuit proof. The later comparisons have separate purposes: [§11.1](#positive-temperature-route) gives another classical input; [§11.2](#fixed-word-probability) adds a second-moment sampling theorem; and [§§11.3–11.5](#depth-quantifiers) compare quantifiers, other models and later finite-size estimates. They are not further premises of the proof just completed.

### 11.2 What is averaged, and a fixed-word probability consequence The probability conclusion here uses an additional fixed-word second-moment theorem, beyond the expected-value construction of §§8.1–8.6. The theorem in §8 is an existence statement about limiting expected energy. There are two random choices behind that expectation. First the couplings $J$ are sampled; then a computational-basis measurement of the state produces a spin string $\Sigma$. For the single word $W$ already chosen, put $$ E_n(J,\Sigma)=H_{n,J}(\Sigma)/n,\qquad \overline E_n(J)=\mathbb E[E_n(J,\Sigma)\mid J]. $$ The quantity defining $v_W$ is $\mathbb E_J\overline E_n(J)$. It is neither the energy of every measured string nor a worst-disorder guarantee. The temporary Gaussian labels used during synthesis are not an extra source of randomness in the final angle vectors. Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann and Zhou supply that additional input. They prove, with the same Hamiltonian and gate-sign convention, that for every fixed word $$ \mathbb E_{J,\Sigma}E_n\longrightarrow v_W, \qquad \mathbb E_{J,\Sigma}E_n^2\longrightarrow v_W^2. $$ Their second expression is the quantum expectation of $(C_{n,J}/n)^2$ averaged over disorder, not merely the square of the conditional mean. Consequently $$ \mathbb E_{J,\Sigma}(E_n-v_W)^2\longrightarrow0, \qquad \Pr_{J,\Sigma}(|E_n-v_W|>s)\longrightarrow0 \quad(s>0). $$ The law of total variance separates what vanishes: $$ \mathbb E(E_n-v_W)^2= \mathbb E_J\operatorname{Var}(E_n\mid J) +\mathbb E_J(\overline E_n(J)-v_W)^2. $$ Both terms are nonnegative and hence tend to zero. Concentration of the conditional mean alone would not control a measured string. This is the elementary second-moment deduction from [Farhi et al., arXiv:1910.08187v4, §4, equations (13)–(22)][fggz]. Now run the circuit construction with accuracy $\varepsilon/2$ and freeze its resulting word. Since $v_W\ge P_*-\varepsilon/2$, $$ \Pr_{J,\Sigma}\{E_n0$, $$ \Pr_J\{b_n(J)>\tau\} \le\mathbb E_J b_n(J)/\tau\longrightarrow0. $$ Thus the same word also has small conditional measurement-failure probability for most disorder instances, in this precise sense. No claim is made for every instance, for arbitrarily varying depths, or with a quantitative size threshold. For $K$ fresh state preparations at the same disorder instance, the conditional failures are independent, so their joint failure probability is $\mathbb E_J b_n(J)^K$, not $(\mathbb E_J b_n(J))^K$. A fraction $\alpha$ of instances that always fail gives $\alpha$ for the former at every $K$. A bound $b_n(J)\le\tau$ on a particular instance does give $\tau^K$ there. Repeatedly measuring an already collapsed state is a different experiment.

**Comparison with the same finite instance.** The concentration of the finite maximum in §11.1.2 strengthens this to a near-optimal sampled configuration. For every $\varepsilon>0$, there is one finite deterministic word $W$, independent of $n$ and $J$, such that $$ \Pr_{J,\Sigma}\!\left\{ H_{n,J}(\Sigma)\ge\max_\sigma H_{n,J}(\sigma)-\varepsilon n \right\}\longrightarrow1. $$ To see this, choose the word with $v_W\ge P_*-\varepsilon/4$ and write $r_n=\mathbb E(E_n-v_W)^2\to0$ and $M_n=\max_\sigma H_{n,J}(\sigma)/n$. The convergence $\mathbb E M_n\to P_*$ makes its bias at most $\varepsilon/4$ for all sufficiently large $n$. The Gaussian coefficient-vector bound from §11.1.2 and Chebyshev's inequality for $E_n$ then give, for $n\ge2$, $$ \Pr_J\{M_n>P_*+\varepsilon/2\} \le2\exp\!\left\{-\frac{n^2\varepsilon^2}{16(n-1)}\right\}, \qquad \Pr_{J,\Sigma}\{E_n

### 11.3 Depth, angle choice and the order of quantifiers The complete witness is a finite ordered word, including every real angle. Its existence for each error tolerance asserts uniformity in system size and disorder that fixed-instance convergence does not provide. The quantifiers should be read literally. The source theorem says that for every $\varepsilon>0$, there is one finite word $W_\varepsilon$ such that $$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb E E_n(W_\varepsilon)\ge P_*-\varepsilon. $$ The cost operator uses $J,n$, but this word and its angles do not. In fixed-instance QAOA convergence, by contrast, the chosen depth and angles may depend on the fixed finite cost matrix and the requested accuracy. The performance of a prescribed family of nonzero angles with $p=p(n)\to\infty$ needs further estimates. A depth allowance alone can be met by the padded existence construction below. The distinction already occurs for the elementary array $a_{n,p}=p/(n+p)$. For each fixed $n$, its limit as $p\to\infty$ is one; for each fixed $p$, its limit as $n\to\infty$ is zero. This is a quantifier example, not a model of QAOA. The finite-dimensional convergence theorem of [Binkowski, Koßmann, Ziegler and Schwonnek, arXiv:2302.04968v1, Theorem 12][binkowski] fixes the optimization problem before selecting a sufficiently long circuit. It does not replace the construction of a size-independent word here. **An existential schedule under a prescribed depth allowance.** There is a narrower diagonal consequence for sampled output. Choose $W_k$ with $P_*-1/k\le v_{W_k}\le P_*$. Fixed-word second-moment convergence supplies $N_k$ so that, for every $n\ge N_k$, $\mathbb E(E_n(W_k)-v_{W_k})^2\le k^{-2}$. Given any prescribed integer depth allowance $d(n)\to\infty$, enlarge these strictly increasing thresholds until $d(n)\ge\operatorname{depth}(W_k)$ for every $n\ge N_k$. On $N_k\le n **Computational meaning of a finite word.** Nor does a supremum over angles assert that an optimizing angle vector exists at any particular depth. The proof constructs a sufficiently good word directly; monotonicity from identity padding then gives the limit of $Q_p$. Each QAOA round contains a full cost evolution and a mixer evolution. In the dense SK model a cost evolution involves all $\binom n2$ pair couplings, so the round count is not itself a bound on two-qubit gate depth, connectivity cost, precision or physical runtime. Three computational questions remain distinct. Evaluating the limiting energy at supplied angles is one task; finding suitable angles is another; implementing and sampling the resulting quantum circuit is a third. The [Basso et al. iteration][bfmvz] evaluates the fixed-angle limit in $O(p^2 4^p)$ arithmetic time. That is not a bound on the search needed to find the existence theorem's angles. Spin–boson representations provide another route to evaluation. The earlier [Boulebnane et al. mapping, arXiv:2505.07929v2][spin-boson], and the later [mixed-spin decoupling paper, arXiv:2609.40309v1, §§II–III and Supplement S2.1][decoupling], must be distinguished: the latter is a separate work, not the reference called BKL2026 in the original QAOA manuscript. Its fixed-depth mapping and numerical tensor-network performance do not supply an efficient angle-selection theorem for the present construction. Its discussion also gives fixed-word finite-size estimates; the absence of a finite-size rate **in the construction here** is not a claim that the wider literature contains none. **Why the two-spin hypothesis matters.** The statement is specific to the quadratic, zero-field SK model. The pure even higher-spin model has a different thermodynamic-first conclusion. For every even interaction order $q\ge4$, [Basso, Gamarnik, Mei and Zhou, arXiv:2204.10306v2, Theorem 4, (3.15), and its proof in §4.2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.10306v2) show $$ v_p^{(q)}(\boldsymbol\theta,\boldsymbol\beta) \le\eta_{\mathrm{OGP}}(G_q)<\eta_{\mathrm{OPT}}(G_q) $$ for every finite $p$ and every fixed angle vector, in that source's normalization. The same ceiling bounds their supremum over all finite $p$ and angles. The proof combines its dense–sparse value identity with the coupled-overlap-gap obstruction of [Chou, Love, Sandhu and Shi, arXiv:2108.06049v3, Parameter 4.1 and Corollary 4.4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.06049v3). That local-algorithm obstruction applies to sparse random signed Max-$q$-XOR for even $q\ge4$, at sufficiently large fixed degree and under the source's logarithmic-depth bound. The Basso–Gamarnik–Mei–Zhou transfer above only needs the resulting obstruction at each fixed depth. It requires no interchange of depth and system size. The exclusion $q\ge4$ is essential; this is not an obstruction for the SK two-spin model treated here. For comparison, [Goh, arXiv:2404.06087v6, Theorem 4.2 and Corollary 4.2.1][goh], treats even interaction order at least four. Its logarithmic-depth obstruction concerns sparse random-regular Max-q-XORSAT; the dense spin-glass corollary is explicitly conditional on swapping limits. The source states on p. 12 that its sparse/dense equivalence is only established at fixed depth, so it does not prove a dense logarithmic-depth obstruction. These hypotheses do not include quadratic SK. Neither a conclusion for all mixed spin glasses nor a general quantum advantage follows from §8. ### 11.4 The regular-MaxCut consequence has its own limits The original manuscript also gives a consequence for MaxCut. For each $\eta>0$ it selects one finite depth and normalized angles, and then a degree threshold, such that every finite simple unweighted $(D+1)$-regular graph of girth greater than $2p+1$ has expected cut fraction at least $$ \frac12+\frac{P_*-\eta}{\sqrt D} $$ for all sufficiently large $D$. The usual MaxCut cost is $H_{\rm MC}=\frac12\sum_{\{i,j\}}(I-Z_iZ_j)$, so its angles are $2\boldsymbol\gamma/\sqrt D$: the normalized angles are fixed, while these physical cost angles depend on degree. The sign conversion uses a bipartition of the relevant tree neighbourhood of each edge; the whole graph need not be bipartite. The further optimality comparison is for a uniform simple labelled $(D+1)$-regular graph $G_{n,D+1}$, along sizes with $n(D+1)$ even. Write $\operatorname{OPT}(G)$ for the maximum cut size divided by $|E(G)|$, $q_{p,G}$ for the circuit's expected cut fraction, and $\Delta_D(G)=\operatorname{OPT}(G)-q_{p,G}(2\boldsymbol\gamma/\sqrt D, \boldsymbol\beta)$. The same word can be chosen so that $$ \lim_{D\to\infty} \limsup_{\substack{n\to\infty\\n(D+1)\ \mathrm{even}}} \Pr_G\{\sqrt D\,\Delta_D(G_{n,D+1})>\eta\}=0. $$ Size goes to infinity first at fixed degree and word. The probability is over the random graph; the cut fraction has already averaged the quantum measurement. For fixed $D,p$, [McKay, Wormald and Wysocka (2004), Theorem 1](https://doi.org/10.37236/1819), gives tight counts of cycles of lengths at most $2p+3$. Every edge with a nontree neighbourhood is within bounded distance of one of these cycles, so their fraction tends to zero. The optimum is supplied separately by [Dembo, Montanari and Sen, arXiv:1503.03923v2, Theorem 1.6(b)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.03923v2): dividing their cut size per vertex by $(D+1)/2$ gives the leading cut fraction $1/2+P_*/\sqrt{D+1}$, with an error $o(D^{-1/2})$ in the stated iterated regime. A high-girth lower bound alone would not prove optimality on every high-girth graph. See [OpenAI (2026b), Corollary 1.2 and its complete proof][q-maxcut]. This separate consequence is recorded to preserve the source's scope; it is not a new selected formal endpoint or a joint size–degree limit.

The full-support theorem and scalar-value theorem use related but
different formal representations. Their mathematical conclusions can be
discussed together, but a direct formal implication would require the
coefficient, Brownian law, control value and diffusion translations
described in §12, with common witnesses. The finite Gaussian result
also needs its rooted energy identification before it says anything
about a QAOA circuit. The boundedness, regularization, synthesis and
transfer estimates in §8 are additional steps, with temperature-specific
hypotheses where the positive-temperature route is used.

Infinite support allows gaps. An indefinite curvature identity does not imply
strict convexity before expectation is controlled. An algebraic certificate
does not establish its analytic hypotheses. Coordinatewise convergence does
not control a growing coefficient sum. A finite-dimensional Gaussian law
does not identify an energy observable without its operator argument.
Separate witnesses cannot be merged silently. The order
$\forall\varepsilon\ \exists\text{finite word}\ \lim_{n\to\infty}$
cannot be replaced by a fixed-instance depth limit.

The local comparison in §11.1 concerns two printed finite-step displays;
it neither replaces the cited theorem's hypotheses nor supplies the
remaining circuit estimates.

The source collection retains the two manuscripts, formal statements,

### 5.3 A fixed QAOA circuit before the thermodynamic limit The remaining consequence uses a separate circuit approximation theorem, stated as Proposition 5 below. We give its finite Gaussian input and identify the energy it approximates. Its operator and control construction is developed in the companion; the support and density proofs above do not require those additional prerequisites. Let $\widehat Z_i,\widehat X_i$ be Pauli operators, and define the cost and mixer by $$ C_{n,J}=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i0$ there is one finite $W$ with $v(W)\geq P_*-\varepsilon$, whose depth and angles depend on $\varepsilon$ but not on $n$ or $J$. The instance still determines $C_{n,J}$. Here depth counts global cost–mixer layers; their elementary gate counts depend on the implementation. This order of limits differs from the fixed-instance depth limit in [Farhi, Goldstone and Gutmann, §VI][FGG], which permits instance-dependent choices. The common-circuit conclusion was conjectured by [Basso, Farhi, Marwaha, Villalonga and Zhou (2022), §7, equation (7.2)][BFMVZ]. **The finite Gaussian input.** Fix the minimiser and its diffusion, a cutoff $0[long §7, “A finite Gaussian spin and its adjacent correlations”](../long/reasoning-record.md#finite-gaussian-approximation). **Proposition 5 (circuit approximation; a consequence of [OpenAI (2026b), §§2–5][Q]).** For each fixed $T,N$ in the preceding construction with finite positive normalisers, and every $\eta>0$, there is a finite ordinary QAOA word $W$, with deterministic angles independent of $n$ and $J$, such that $$ |v(W)-S_{T,N}|<\eta. $$ **Why the adjacent pairing is the energy.** We use the rooted Gaussian representation of [OpenAI (2026b), §2 and Lemma 3.1][Q], building on the spin–boson description of [Boulebnane et al. (2026)][spin-boson]. Its classical sector consists of square-integrable functions built recursively from a local Gaussian seed and child-generated Gaussian coordinates, with inner product given by expectation. For any finite list of fixed centred real child directions, their coordinates at the receiving root have a joint centred Gaussian law. For two such directions $f,g$, $$ \mathbb E[\mathsf G(f)\mathsf G(g)]=\langle f,g\rangle. $$ The directions are fixed elements of the child space, even when their values depend on the child's Gaussian coordinates. The receiving root's seed is independent of these coordinates; compatible embeddings preserve them as the recursive depth grows. The root shift $\mathsf L$ inserts a child direction into the first Gaussian chaos (the linear Gaussian part) with constant receiving-root state. Its adjoint projects onto that part and returns the child direction. The [one-pair calculation at the start of long §8](../long/reasoning-record.md#depth-one-calibration) checks this representation's energy against the finite SK circuit before the general construction in §8.1. Start with a standard normal receiving-root seed $g_0$ and recursively put $Z_{j+1}=\mathsf G(g_j)$. The orthonormal child directions give independent standard Gaussian lifts, reproducing the scalar law. The finite spin $F_N$ depends only on those lifts. Projection therefore gives the exact rooted-energy identity $$ \begin{aligned} \mathsf L^*F_N&=\sum_{j=0}^N\mathbb E[F_NZ_{j+1}]g_j,\\ \mathcal E(F_N):=\operatorname{Re}\langle F_N,\mathsf L F_N\rangle &=\sum_{j=0}^N\mathbb E[F_Ng_j]\,\mathbb E[F_NZ_{j+1}] =S_{T,N}. \end{aligned} \tag{12} $$ Independence of the receiving-root seed removes the $j=0$ term. This identity concerns the finite Gaussian formula in a limiting rooted space, not a finite-$n$ circuit. The unshifted pairing can have the same scalar limit without identifying this energy. The construction and projection are proved in [long §8.1](../long/reasoning-record.md#rooted-energy). The shift records the lift from a child direction $g_j$ to the receiving coordinate $Z_{j+1}$. A one-step example distinguishes it from the unshifted pairing. For the nonminimising heat coefficient $\gamma=0$, take $T=4/5$ and $N=1$. Then $g_1=Z_1$ and $F_1=\operatorname{sgn}(2Z_1+Z_2)$, so Gaussian regression gives $$ S_{T,1}=\frac4{5\pi},\qquad \mathbb E[F_1g_1]\,\mathbb E[F_1Z_1]=\frac8{5\pi}. $$ This tests the finite representation, not the minimiser-dependent limit in (11). The calculation is in [long §10.4, “An exact one-step calculation”](../long/reasoning-record.md#one-step-example). **Construction underlying Proposition 5.** [OpenAI (2026b), §§3–5][Q] smooths the spin and approximates every transmitted function by a bounded smooth map, preserving oddness; smoothing the final sign alone is insufficient. Its class exclusions prevent return through a traversed branch and reserve helper classes on which the output is zero, with positive probabilities fixed during synthesis. The resulting finite formula is approximated in energy using temporary Gaussian controls, with the same sitewise seeds throughout the word. Removing those controls produces an ordinary word, whose limiting energy is $v(W)$ by the fixed-word transfer. The approximation errors are absolute and can be chosen successively for each fixed $S_{T,N}$, before it is chosen close to $P_*$. The preserved quantity is energy; the measured-configuration conclusion below uses a further concentration theorem. The complete error bound is in [long §8.6, finite-formula energy approximation](../long/reasoning-record.md#finite-formula-energy-error), with the constructions and their hypotheses in [long §§8.1–8.6](../long/reasoning-record.md#qaoa-construction). The deduction of near-optimality is now explicit: $$ P_*-v(W)\leq (P_*-I_T)+|I_T-S_{T,N}|+|S_{T,N}-v(W)|. \tag{13} $$ Choose $T$ so that $1-T<\varepsilon/3$, then $N$ so that the second term is below $\varepsilon/3$, and finally use Proposition 5 with $\eta<\varepsilon/3$. These finite choices give $v(W)>P_*-\varepsilon$ before $n$ tends to infinity. The source's Appendix A supplies an alternative positive-temperature input to the same synthesis. This construction supplies no bounds on depth or cost-angle magnitudes in terms of accuracy, and no efficient procedure for finding angles. A separate estimate for the expected energy of a specified word is described in [long §11.5](../long/reasoning-record.md#finite-size-comparison). Its threshold depends on the word's depth and cost angles. Without bounds on those parameters it gives no threshold in optimisation accuracy alone; it also supplies no rate for measurement concentration. **Corollary 6 (a measured configuration on the same instance).** For every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite ordinary QAOA word $W_\varepsilon$, chosen independently of $n$ and $J$, such that one computational-basis measurement $\Sigma$ satisfies $$ \Pr_{J,\Sigma}\!\left\{ \max_\sigma H_{n,J}(\sigma)-H_{n,J}(\Sigma)\leq\varepsilon n \right\}\longrightarrow1 \qquad(n\to\infty). \tag{14} $$ **Proof.** For a fixed word, put $Y_n=H_{n,J}(\Sigma)/n$ and $K_n=\max_\sigma H_{n,J}(\sigma)/n$. [Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann and Zhou, §4, equations (13)–(22)][FGGZ] prove $$ \mathbb E_{J,\Sigma}Y_n\to v(W),\qquad \mathbb E_{J,\Sigma}Y_n^2\to v(W)^2. $$ The second moment is $\mathbb E_J\langle(C_{n,J}/n)^2\rangle$, so it includes measurement variance as well as disorder fluctuations. Thus $Y_n\to v(W)$ in joint $L^2$. Gaussian concentration of the maximum and its defining mean limit give $K_n\to P_*$ in probability. Choose $W$ with $P_*-v(W)<\varepsilon/3$. With probability tending to one, both $K_n-P_*<\varepsilon/3$ and $v(W)-Y_n<\varepsilon/3$, which proves (14). The two energies use the same $J$; no independence between them is needed. The companion's [§11.2, “What is averaged, and a fixed-word probability consequence”](../long/reasoning-record.md#fixed-word-probability) gives the concentration argument and its further probability consequences.
